hero.headline: Microsoft AI chief calls Anthropic models too expensive
hero.body:
Microsoft Supports Anthropic's Legal Challenge Against Pentagon

Microsoft has filed a court brief backing Anthropic's legal challenge against a Pentagon designation that has effectively blocked the AI company from government work. The filing, submitted to federal court in San Francisco this week, argues that a temporary restraining order is necessary to prevent disruption to suppliers whose products depend on Anthropic's technology.

Google, Amazon, Apple and OpenAI have also signed onto a brief supporting Anthropic. In a statement, Microsoft said: "The Department of War needs reliable access to the country's best technology. And everyone wants to ensure AI is not used for mass domestic surveillance or to start a war without human control. The government, the entire tech sector, and the American public need a path to achieve all these goals together."

Anthropic launched two lawsuits Monday, one in federal court in California and one in the DC circuit court of appeals, challenging the Pentagon's decision to label the company a supply-chain risk. This designation has never before been applied to a US company. The dispute emerged after contract negotiations collapsed last month over a $200 million deal to deploy Anthropic's AI on classified military systems. Anthropic insisted its technology should not be used for mass surveillance of US citizens or to power autonomous lethal weapons. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth then designated the company a supply-chain risk, and Anthropic says its government contracts have already begun to be cancelled.

Pentagon chief technology officer Emil Michael told CNBC on Thursday that "there's no chance" the agency will renegotiate with Anthropic after the designation.

In its legal complaint, Anthropic explained the reasoning behind its restrictions. "Anthropic currently does not have confidence, for example, that Claude would function reliably or safely if used to support lethal autonomous warfare," the filing stated. "These usage restrictions are therefore rooted in Anthropic's unique understanding of Claude's risks and limitations."

The company also argued that its First Amendment rights were under attack, contending that the Pentagon used the supply-chain risk designation, typically reserved for firms with ties to foreign adversaries like China, as ideological punishment for its public stance on AI safety.

Microsoft is one of the Pentagon's most deeply embedded tech partners. The company holds a share of the military's $9 billion Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability contract alongside Amazon, Google and Oracle, plus separate software and enterprise services deals worth several billion dollars more. Under the Trump administration in September, Microsoft struck another multibillion-dollar deal to help advance cloud services and AI in the federal government.

Meanwhile, House Democrats have pressed the Pentagon for information about whether artificial intelligence, including the Maven Smart System, was used to identify targets in recent military strikes in Iran that have resulted in civilian casualties.

cards.headline: House passes Ukraine aid and Russia sanctions over Trump opposition
cards.body:
The House of Representatives approved legislation providing aid to Ukraine and imposing sanctions on key segments of the Russian economy in a 226-195 vote on Thursday, marking the second major foreign policy break with Donald Trump in a week.

The vote represents significant congressional pushback against Trump's approach to the war in Ukraine. Republican leaders, aligned with Trump's position, had warned members that the bill would undermine negotiations they believed could achieve comparable but stronger results. Despite these objections, enough Republican lawmakers joined Democrats to pass the measure.

The passage comes just one day after the House voted for the first time to approve a war powers resolution aimed at halting U.S. military action against Iran. Together, these votes signal congressional impatience with Trump's foreign policy direction and suggest limits to his influence over the Republican caucus on international matters.

The legislation addresses Ukraine's ongoing defense needs as the conflict continues. The sanctions component targets Russian economic interests in response to the invasion. Supporters of the bill have argued that aiding Ukraine serves American national security interests by opposing Russian territorial expansion and supporting a democratic ally against authoritarian aggression.

The debate reflects divisions within the Republican Party over U.S. foreign policy commitments. Some GOP members advocate for reducing American involvement abroad, aligning with Trump's position, while others maintain that supporting Ukraine against Russia remains strategically important. The successful passage of Thursday's bill demonstrates that a working coalition exists in the House to advance Ukraine assistance regardless of Trump's opposition.

The vote also arrives as Europe takes parallel steps to support Ukraine. The European Union recently completed a 90 billion euro loan agreement for Ukraine after Hungary lifted its veto, and the bloc finalized its 20th sanctions package against Russia. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated that while "Russia doubles down on its aggression, we are doubling down on our support to the brave Ukrainian nation."

The U.S. House legislation now moves to the Senate for consideration, where its fate remains uncertain. Democratic lawmakers have expressed strong support for the measure, framing it as necessary to counter Russian aggression. The breadth and durability of the pro-Ukraine coalition in Congress will be tested as additional votes approach on related foreign policy matters.

The repeated congressional breaks with Trump on Ukraine and Iran policy suggest that despite his influence within the Republican Party, significant numbers of GOP representatives are willing to vote against his positions on major international issues. This pattern may shape the dynamics of foreign policy debates for the remainder of the congressional session.

cards.headline: Zelensky proposes direct talks with Putin to end war
cards.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has written an open letter directly to Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling for face-to-face negotiations to end the ongoing conflict. The letter marks the first time Zelensky has publicly addressed Putin in writing since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, and represents a significant diplomatic gesture toward direct engagement between the two leaders.

In the letter, Zelensky argues that only direct talks between Ukraine and Russia can resolve the war. He contends that while Ukrainian resilience remains strong, most Russians have grown weary of the conflict and are ready for peace. The proposal suggests holding talks in a neutral third country.

The timing of Zelensky's initiative coincides with shifting diplomatic priorities in Washington. With the United States focusing its efforts on Iran rather than Ukraine, Kyiv appears to be taking a more independent approach to seeking resolution directly with Moscow, rather than relying primarily on Western mediation.

The Kremlin has not yet publicly responded to Zelensky's proposal. Previous high-level negotiations between Ukrainian and Russian leaders have achieved limited results, with both sides maintaining fundamentally incompatible positions on territorial control and security guarantees.

Any potential meeting would represent the most significant direct diplomatic contact between the two leaders since the war began. However, analysts say a breakthrough remains unlikely given current circumstances. Both armies show signs of exhaustion while sustaining heavy casualties, and the conflict continues to devastate Ukraine's energy infrastructure through ongoing strikes.

The prospects for productive talks face substantial obstacles. The Kremlin continues to demand that Ukraine withdraw its troops from the Donbas region as a precondition for negotiations. Ukraine has flatly rejected any suggestion that it unilaterally withdraw from its own territory, a position strengthened by recent battlefield dynamics in which Russian advances have largely stalled.

Germany's defence minister, Boris Pistorius, expressed skepticism about Putin's apparent interest in peace discussions. He suggested the Russian leader may be using peace rhetoric as a strategic deception, noting that if Putin genuinely wanted to end the conflict, he could do so himself rather than setting conditions. Pistorius characterized such statements as part of Putin's broader hybrid war strategy aimed at diverting attention from Russian weaknesses.

A US-brokered ceasefire is set to expire, and Moscow has rejected extending the truce. Meanwhile, European Union leaders have sought to secure a role in any future substantive peace negotiations, insisting that Ukraine must remain involved in all discussions and decisions about its own future.

Success in any talks would depend on whether both leaders prove willing to make significant concessions on core issues including territorial control, security arrangements, and Ukraine's international alignment. Given the heavy investments both sides have made in military operations and their opposing positions, the path forward remains highly uncertain.

cards.headline: Hezbollah rejects Israel-Lebanon ceasefire brokered by US
cards.teaser: The Iran-backed group says it was excluded from negotiations and calls the agreement a surrender.
cards.body:
Hezbollah has rejected a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon announced by the United States on Wednesday following fresh rounds of talks. The Iran-backed group, which was excluded from the US-brokered negotiations between Israel and the Lebanese government, views the truce as a surrender of its interests.

The rejection raises questions about the ceasefire's viability, given Hezbollah's significant military and political influence in Lebanon. Fighting has continued between the two sides, with exchanges of strikes ongoing. A UN peacekeeper was killed and others wounded by mortar fire in southeastern Lebanon as violence persisted.

cards.headline: Xi Jinping to visit North Korea for talks with Kim Jong Un
cards.teaser: The Chinese president will travel to North Korea from June 8 to 9 in a rare visit to the isolated country.
cards.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping will visit North Korea next week for meetings with leader Kim Jong Un, marking a rare trip by a foreign head of state to the isolated regime. The visit is scheduled to last from June 8 to 9.

The meeting between the two leaders comes at a time of heightened attention to North Korean diplomacy and regional security dynamics in East Asia. China remains North Korea's most important economic partner and diplomatic ally, and high-level visits between the two countries signal the strength of their relationship.

cards.headline: House committee passes $1.15 trillion defense bill after 14-hour session
cards.body:
The House of Representatives voted 312-112 on Wednesday to approve a sweeping defense policy bill that authorizes $900 billion in military programs for the coming year. The 3,000-page legislation, known as the National Defense Authorization Act, includes significant provisions for troop compensation, weapons procurement reforms, and continued support for Ukraine.

The bill provides a 3.8 percent pay raise for many military members and funds improvements to military housing and facilities. It also overhauls how the Department of Defense purchases weapons, emphasizing speed after years of delays from the defense industry.

The legislation maintains a strong U.S. military presence in Europe by requiring the Pentagon to keep at least 76,000 troops and major equipment stationed there unless NATO allies are consulted. The bill also sets a minimum requirement of 28,500 troops in South Korea. Additionally, it authorizes $400 million for each of the next two years to manufacture weapons for Ukraine, demonstrating congressional commitment to supporting the country against Russian aggression.

The bill includes a controversial provision regarding boat strikes in the Caribbean targeting suspected drug smugglers. It demands that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth provide Congress with full, unedited video of a September strike near Venezuela that killed survivors of an earlier strike. The legislation withholds part of Hegseth's travel budget until the Pentagon releases this footage and allows Congress to review the orders for the strikes.

The measure makes significant cuts aligned with the Trump administration's priorities. It reduces climate-related spending by $1.6 billion, reversing years of military investment in addressing climate change as a national security threat. The bill also cuts $40 million in funding for diversity, equity, and inclusion programs.

Congress is formally ending the war in Iraq by repealing the 2003 authorization for the invasion. Supporters say the repeal prevents future abuses and reinforces that Iraq is now a strategic partner. The legislation also permanently removes U.S. sanctions on Syria imposed in 2019, allowing international companies to invest in reconstruction efforts under the new Syrian government.

The bill strikes bipartisan compromises on several issues. While cutting climate and diversity efforts, it boosts congressional oversight of the Pentagon and includes provisions to keep U.S. troops stationed abroad. However, the legislation faced criticism from some senators regarding military flight restrictions over Washington following a deadly midair collision earlier this year between an Army helicopter and a commercial jetliner near Ronald Reagan National Airport.

Democrats criticized Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson for stripping a provision to expand in vitro fertilization coverage for active duty military personnel.

The White House has signaled support for the legislation, which now heads to the Senate for consideration before lawmakers depart for the holiday break.

cards.headline: Trump directs $700 million into coal using wartime authority
cards.teaser: The president invoked emergency powers to fund coal investment as the Iran conflict drives up energy costs for American consumers.
cards.body:
President Trump announced a $700 million investment in coal production, using wartime powers to direct federal funds to the industry. The administration cited rising energy prices stemming from the ongoing conflict with Iran as justification for the move.

The decision represents a significant federal intervention in energy markets using emergency authorities during the geopolitical crisis. Coal has faced a declining role in America's energy sector in recent years.

cards.headline: Albania sees days of protests over Kushner-backed resort project
cards.teaser: A luxury resort plan supported by Jared Kushner has sparked demonstrations and raised European Union concerns.
cards.body:
Demonstrations have erupted across Albania in opposition to a luxury resort development linked to Jared Kushner. Environmental campaigners and local critics argue the coastal project would damage a protected environment and harm the country's pristine coastline.

The government has promoted the development as transformative for the nation, while the European Union has raised concerns about the use of the unspoiled coastal areas. The protests underscore the growing tension between economic development plans and environmental protection in Albania.

cards.headline: Sherpa guide found alive on Everest after family begins funeral rites
cards.teaser: A guide missing for a week on Mount Everest was discovered crawling toward base camp while his family had started funeral ceremonies.
cards.body:
A Sherpa guide who went missing on Mount Everest has been found alive after six days alone on the mountain. Dawa Sherpa was discovered by cleaners crawling toward Base Camp, where his family had already begun funeral rites believing he had died.

Sherpa became separated from climber Chris Thrall during their expedition. His survival through nearly a week in Everest's extreme conditions surprised rescue teams and marked a remarkable self-rescue on the world's highest peak.

cards.headline: Ex-wife of Dubai ruler's nephew detained, prosecutors say
cards.teaser: Zeynab Javadli has been in custody and out of contact with friends since Tuesday, according to authorities.
cards.body:
Prosecutors have confirmed that Zeynab Javadli, the former wife of a nephew of Dubai's ruler, is in custody. Javadli had not been in contact with any of her friends since Tuesday, raising concern among her social circle before authorities confirmed her detention.

The reasons for her detention and the charges she may face have not been disclosed by prosecutors. The case has drawn attention due to Javadli's connection to Dubai's ruling family through her former marriage.

cards.headline: US to deploy sterile flies and dogs to fight screwworm outbreak
cards.teaser: The flesh-eating insect has appeared in America for the first time since 1966, prompting a coordinated response in southern states.
cards.body:
The United States is mobilizing to combat a flesh-eating screwworm outbreak using sterile flies and detection dogs. The parasitic insect, absent from America since 1966, has reappeared and is spreading concern across the southern United States.

Screwworm larvae consume living tissue and pose serious risks to livestock and humans. Authorities will deploy sterile male flies to disrupt the insects' reproduction—a technique that successfully eradicated the pest decades ago. Detection dogs will help identify infected animals quickly, limiting further spread of the infestation.

cards.headline: Senate rejects efforts to block Trump's $1.8 billion settlement fund
cards.teaser: Republicans defeated multiple amendments aimed at limiting or eliminating a $1.8 billion fund tied to a Trump settlement during an overnight Senate session.
cards.body:
Senate Republicans narrowly blocked a Democratic attempt to stop President Trump from creating a $1.8 billion fund to pay his allies. Democratic leader Chuck Schumer had proposed language to bar the payouts as part of Republican-backed legislation funding Trump's mass deportation campaign.

The vote revealed growing dissent within the Republican party over the proposal. Three GOP senators joined Democrats in opposing the fund, which Trump's supporters have described as an "anti-weaponization" measure. The fund could potentially issue financial settlements to people connected to the January 6 insurrection.

cards.headline: Nithya Raman gains ground on Rick Pratt in Los Angeles mayor race
cards.teaser: City Councilmember Nithya Raman has narrowed the gap with developer Rick Pratt for second place in the Los Angeles mayoral primary, with many ballots still uncounted.
cards.body:
Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman has closed in on developer Rick Pratt in the race for second place in the city's mayoral primary, though a substantial number of ballots remain to be counted. The two are competing to advance to a November runoff against the current leader. Second place in the primary determines who will face the frontrunner in the general election.

Mayor Karen Bass has already secured a spot in the November runoff as the top vote-getter in the primary. The remaining question is whether Raman can overtake Pratt to become the second candidate in the general election matchup. Final results will depend on the counting of outstanding ballots in the coming days.

cards.headline: Multiple women accuse Graham Platner of unsettling behavior
cards.teaser: Several women who dated Graham Platner have come forward with allegations of troubling conduct, including new claims about Nazi tattoos, roiling his political campaign.
cards.body:
Graham Platner, a Democratic candidate for US Senate in Maine, has rejected allegations of abusive behavior toward women published in a New York Times article. The report included an interview with a Republican operative who accused him of womanizing, physical misconduct, and making troubling comments about rape. Platner characterized the allegations as "politically motivated."

Platner denied claims of physical abuse, stating the accusations "are simply not true." The controversy has drawn significant media attention as he pursues his Senate campaign in Maine.

cards.headline: Putin says Russia will strengthen air defenses after Ukrainian drone strikes
cards.teaser: President Vladimir Putin announced plans to bolster Russian air defenses in response to Ukrainian drone attacks that have reached deep into the country.
cards.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin announced plans to strengthen the country's air defense systems in response to recent Ukrainian drone attacks that have penetrated deep into Russian territory. Putin made the statement during the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum in his hometown, an event meant to showcase Russia's economy.

The Ukrainian drone campaign has demonstrated the ability to strike targets far from the front lines, reaching areas previously considered secure. The attacks have cast a shadow over Putin's showcase economic forum, one of Russia's most prominent annual events.

cards.headline: Ukrainian President Zelensky proposes direct talks with Putin
cards.teaser: President Volodymyr Zelensky sent an open letter to Vladimir Putin proposing face-to-face negotiations as the path to ending the war.
cards.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has written an open letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin proposing face-to-face negotiations between the two leaders. Zelensky argues that only direct engagement between Ukraine and Russia can end the war. The timing of the proposal comes as American attention shifts toward Iran, potentially reducing external focus on the Ukraine conflict.

Meanwhile, Putin announced that Russia will strengthen its air defenses in response to recent Ukrainian drone attacks that have penetrated deep into Russian territory, including reaching St. Petersburg during an economic forum in his hometown.

cards.headline: UK military chief warns of most dangerous security period
cards.teaser: Britain's Chief of the Defence Staff said the UK faces its most dangerous period in his experience, citing Russian actions that risk crossing red lines.
cards.body:
Sir Richard Knighton, Chief of the Defence Staff, has told the BBC that the United Kingdom is facing its most dangerous security period in recent times. He cited Russian incursions into UK defences as a key concern, warning that these actions risk crossing a line that could provoke a serious confrontation.

The assessment reflects escalating tensions between Russia and Western nations. Knighton's warning highlights growing alarm among British defence leadership over the security landscape, particularly regarding Russian military activities near NATO member states.

hero.headline: S&P blocks SpaceX from early entry into benchmark index
hero.body:
S&P Dow Jones Indices has declined to modify its rules to permit SpaceX early admission to its benchmark index, preventing the rocket company from joining the S&P 500 before its highly anticipated initial public offering. The decision upholds existing eligibility standards that typically require companies to be publicly traded for a specified period before consideration for index inclusion.

SpaceX is preparing to launch what would be the largest initial public offering in history, seeking $75 billion in its public debut. The company has committed to its planned $135 per share IPO price and will not adjust this valuation. JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon is personally involved in pitching the offering to investors, with banks preparing to collect substantial fees from the historic deal.

Index funds had begun preparing for SpaceX's potential inclusion by allocating space in their portfolios for the company's shares. The S&P's decision to maintain standard rules means SpaceX must now meet conventional eligibility criteria before it can be added to the index. This development affects both the company and passive funds that track S&P indices.

Retail investors had anticipated a significant buying surge if index funds were required to purchase SpaceX shares following early index entry. That scenario has now been eliminated. Following the announcement, other space-related stocks experienced declines in overnight trading as the expected positive spillover effect from index-driven purchases failed to occur.

The company has established a dedicated website to reach retail investors ahead of next week's public offering. If successful, the IPO would value SpaceX at more than $200 billion. Industry observers expect the listing to increase Elon Musk's net worth past $1 trillion. The offering represents a significant test for public markets, which have seen relatively few mega-deals of comparable size in recent years.

The index provider's refusal to create an exception surprised some market participants who had expected SpaceX might receive special treatment given the unprecedented scale of its upcoming offering. However, S&P maintained that existing rules would apply without modification.

The decision underscores how even the largest and most prominent companies must follow standard procedures for index inclusion rather than receive preferential treatment. SpaceX will need to establish a track record as a publicly traded company before becoming eligible for S&P 500 membership.

Industry analysts note that the ruling provides clarity to market participants regarding index methodology and demonstrates that major index providers will not adjust their established criteria, regardless of deal size or company prominence. The SpaceX IPO proceeds as scheduled next week without the added boost that early S&P 500 inclusion would have provided.

cards.headline: China restricts content in viral short drama videos
cards.teaser: Chinese regulators are cracking down on explicit content, violence, and materialism in micro dramas that have surged in popularity.
cards.body:
China has launched a regulatory crackdown targeting micro dramas, the short-form video content that has exploded in popularity across the country. Authorities are focusing on content deemed to contain soft pornography, violence, and materialistic themes that have become common in these viral productions.

The short videos have drawn criticism for sensationalist content even as they have gained massive audiences. Chinese officials say the restrictions are needed to maintain social values and protect viewers from inappropriate material in the rapidly growing format.

cards.headline: China builds economic barriers as global tensions increase
cards.teaser: Beijing is implementing changes it says are needed for national security, but the moves could complicate overseas growth for Chinese companies.
cards.body:
China is constructing what analysts describe as an economic fortress, implementing new barriers and restrictions as tensions with other major economies rise. Beijing has framed the changes as necessary measures to protect national security interests in an increasingly uncertain global environment.

The new policies could create obstacles for Chinese companies seeking to expand into foreign markets. While Chinese officials say the measures are defensive in nature, they represent a significant shift in how the country manages its economic relationships with the rest of the world and may limit growth opportunities for domestic firms looking beyond China's borders.

cards.headline: South Korean stocks drop 5% following Wall Street tech sell-off
cards.teaser: Technology stocks in South Korea fell sharply as the country's market followed a plunge in AI-linked names on Wall Street.
cards.body:
South Korean stocks fell 5% as technology companies tracked a sharp decline in AI-linked stocks on Wall Street. The country's tech-heavy market experienced significant losses, with major technology firms suffering from the broader pullback in artificial intelligence equities.

The sell-off highlights how quickly market movements spread across borders. South Korean tech heavyweights, which have substantial exposure to global AI trends, proved particularly sensitive to the downturn originating in the United States.

cards.headline: Anthropic calls for coordinated plan to halt AI development if risks grow
cards.teaser: The artificial intelligence company says labs need a shared mechanism to stop development if dangers increase beyond acceptable levels.
cards.body:
Anthropic urged artificial intelligence laboratories to create a coordinated plan for halting development if risks from AI systems rise to dangerous levels. The company said the industry needs what it described as a brake pedal that multiple labs could activate together if threats emerge.

The AI developer is calling for a potential global freeze in development under certain circumstances, warning specifically about risks from AI systems that can improve themselves. Anthropic co-founders said the proposal is not meant to cause panic but to establish safeguards before problems arise in the rapidly advancing field.

cards.headline: British Heart Foundation to close 150 charity shops
cards.teaser: The charity says it faces an exceptionally challenging trading environment as it plans widespread store closures.
cards.body:
The British Heart Foundation announced plans to close 150 of its charity shops across the United Kingdom. The organization cited what it called an exceptionally challenging trading environment as the reason for the widespread closures.

The decision represents a significant contraction for one of Britain's largest charity retail operations. The foundation's stores have been a fixture on British high streets for decades, selling donated goods to fund cardiovascular research and support programs.

cards.headline: Anthropic revenue reaches $47 billion ahead of IPO
cards.teaser: The AI company reported annualized revenue crossed $47 billion in May, up from $9 billion at the end of 2025.
cards.body:
Anthropic announced that its annualized revenue crossed $47 billion in May, a significant jump from approximately $9 billion at the end of 2025. The company is preparing for an initial public offering as it continues its rapid expansion.

Co-founder Daniela Amodei has dismissed concerns about returns on artificial intelligence investments. However, the company's impressive growth trajectory will face scrutiny as it transitions to becoming a publicly traded company.

cards.headline: Airbnb CEO plans to launch new AI lab
cards.teaser: Brian Chesky said the company has not yet struck a partnership with an existing large language model provider.
cards.body:
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky has announced plans to establish a new artificial intelligence lab. This move marks the company's shift toward developing its own AI capabilities rather than partnering with external providers.

Previously, Chesky explained that Airbnb had not pursued large language model partnerships because existing products were not sufficiently developed for the company's needs. The new lab suggests Airbnb believes it can better serve its platform by building AI tools in-house.

cards.headline: Former OpenAI executive Mira Murati returns to public view
cards.teaser: The AI executive is stepping back into the spotlight after a period of lower visibility.
cards.body:
Mira Murati, a former OpenAI executive, is stepping back into the spotlight after keeping a lower profile. The return comes at a time when remaining out of public view has diminishing returns in the competitive AI industry.

At some point in the current environment, executives need to make noise to remind the market they exist. Murati's renewed public presence reflects the pressure on AI leaders to maintain visibility as the sector continues to attract intense attention and investment.

cards.headline: Ad blocker Filtr launches feature to block ads in iPhone and Mac apps
cards.teaser: The app can now block ads inside apps, including web browsers, using a new feature in the latest Apple software.
cards.body:
Filtr, a privacy tool for Apple devices, can now block ads from loading inside apps thanks to a new feature in the latest Apple software. The app works on iPhones, iPads, and Macs and previously focused primarily on blocking ads in web browsers.

The expanded capability allows Filtr to block ads across web browsers and other applications, significantly increasing its reach throughout the Apple ecosystem.

cards.headline: Founders Fund launches game show featuring tech executives
cards.teaser: The debut episode included appearances by Sam Altman and Palmer Luckey.
cards.body:
Founders Fund, a prominent venture capital firm, has ventured into entertainment with a new game show featuring leading technology executives. The debut episode brought together notable figures including Sam Altman and Palmer Luckey, showcasing current industry luminaries in an unusual format for a VC firm.

Mike Solana, Founders Fund's chief marketing officer, served as moderator for the program, guiding the interactions between the tech elite participants.

cards.headline: Mangrove forests recover after decades of destruction
cards.teaser: The coastal forests are staging a comeback, with benefits for coastal communities and the climate.
cards.body:
Mangrove forests around the world are making an unexpected recovery after suffering decades of human-driven decline. These coastal wetland ecosystems are bouncing back, offering encouraging signs for both local communities and global environmental efforts.

The restoration of mangrove forests brings multiple benefits. They serve as natural barriers against storms and flooding, protecting coastal populations from severe weather events. Additionally, these forests play an important role in climate action by storing substantial amounts of carbon, making their recovery valuable for addressing climate change.

hero.headline: Yankees lose Aaron Judge to stress fracture in rib
hero.teaser: The Yankees announced that outfielder Aaron Judge has been diagnosed with a stress fracture of the first rib on his right side.
hero.body:
Aaron Judge will miss time after the Yankees diagnosed him with a stress fracture of the first rib on his right side, the team announced Thursday night. The injury to the star outfielder represents a significant blow to New York's lineup.

The Yankees did not provide a timeline for Judge's return. Stress fractures in the rib area can sideline players for extended periods depending on severity. Judge has been one of baseball's premier sluggers since breaking into the majors.

cards.headline: Hurricanes even Stanley Cup Final with overtime win over Golden Knights
cards.teaser: Seth Jarvis scored on the power play 3 minutes and 47 seconds into overtime to give the Carolina Hurricanes a 4-3 victory over the Vegas Golden Knights in Game .
cards.body:
Seth Jarvis scored on the power play 3:56 into overtime to lift the Carolina Hurricanes past the Vegas Golden Knights 4-3 in Game 2 of the Stanley Cup Final on Thursday night. The win evens the series at one game apiece.

Carolina erased a two-goal deficit in the third period, only to allow Vegas to tie the game late in regulation. The thrilling third period saw four goals scored before Jarvis ended the back-and-forth battle with his overtime power-play goal. The series now shifts to Carolina for Games 3 and 4.

cards.headline: Texas wins second consecutive Women's College World Series title
cards.teaser: Kayden Henry homered to lead Texas to a 4-1 victory over Texas Tech for a second straight national championship.
cards.body:
Texas defeated Texas Tech 4-1 on Thursday night at the Women's College World Series to win a second consecutive national championship. Kayden Henry hit a home run that helped the Longhorns secure the victory over their in-state rivals.

The back-to-back titles mark a dominant stretch for the Texas softball program.

cards.headline: Dodgers and Diamondbacks players injured in collision at first base
cards.teaser: Max Muncy and Ildemaro Vargas both left Thursday's game after colliding violently at first base.
cards.body:
Los Angeles Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy and Arizona Diamondbacks first baseman Ildemaro Vargas collided at first base during Thursday's game. Both players left the game following the violent impact.

The specific circumstances of the collision were not detailed in available reports.

cards.headline: Lynx rookie Olivia Miles breaks WNBA record with eight three-pointers
cards.teaser: Minnesota guard Olivia Miles made eight three-pointers Thursday night, breaking the WNBA rookie record that Caitlin Clark tied in 2024.
cards.body:
Lynx guard Olivia Miles broke a WNBA rookie record by making eight three-pointers in Thursday night's game against the Valkyries. The performance surpassed the previous mark set by Caitlin Clark of the Indiana Fever, who tied the record during the 2024 rookie season.

Miles' shooting display demonstrated her range as a first-year player for Minnesota.

cards.headline: Caitlin Clark scores 17 points after vomiting at halftime in Fever win
cards.teaser: Despite feeling ill and vomiting at halftime, Clark played on and finished with 17 points and eight assists in an 83-71 victory over Atlanta.
cards.body:
Caitlin Clark powered through illness to lead the Indiana Fever past the Atlanta Dream 83-71 in their Commissioner's Cup opener. Despite vomiting at halftime, Clark returned to the court and finished with 17 points and eight assists.

The Fever star's performance showcased her determination to contribute to the victory despite feeling unwell during the game.

cards.headline: Jennifer Kupcho leads US Women's Open after first round
cards.teaser: Kupcho holds a one-shot advantage after the opening round of golf's second women's major championship of the year.
cards.body:
Jennifer Kupcho made a strong start at the US Women's Open, taking a one-shot lead after the first round on Thursday. The tournament is the second women's major championship of the year.

Three more rounds remain as Kupcho looks to extend her advantage and claim the title.

hero.headline: Actor James Handy stabbed to death at California home
hero.body:
Veteran actor James Handy, 81, was found dead at his home in Tarzana, California, on Wednesday morning after suffering multiple stab wounds to the chest. The Los Angeles Police Department arrested Michael Gledhill, 44, the son of Handy's girlfriend, in connection with the death.

Police responded to the scene at 9:30am after receiving a 911 call. According to the Los Angeles Police Department statement, the caller said: "I am the son of man, I just killed the man of sin." When officers arrived, Gledhill told them he was "the one they were looking for."

"The suspect resides at the location with his mother, who is the victim's girlfriend," the police statement said. Gledhill has been charged on suspicion of murder, with bail set at 2 million dollars.

Handy was born in New York City and began his acting career in 1977 on the television series Ryan's Hope. He went on to appear in numerous films and television shows across multiple decades. His filmography includes character roles in Jumanji, Top Gun: Maverick, and Logan. He also had credits in K-911, Law and Order, NCIS: Los Angeles, and Criminal Minds. His most recent film appearance was in Top Gun: Maverick in 2022.

The 2022 film brought Handy recognition among new audiences as part of the sequel to the original 1986 Top Gun. He appeared alongside other cast members in supporting roles within the major Hollywood production.

The Los Angeles Police Department is continuing its investigation into the fatal stabbing. The department did not provide additional details about the circumstances that led to the stabbing or the nature of the relationship between Handy and Gledhill beyond their connection through Gledhill's mother.

Handy's death marks the end of a career spanning nearly five decades in entertainment. His work in television and film established him as a character actor known for supporting roles in major productions. The incident at his Tarzana residence has drawn attention to his contributions to Hollywood over his long career in the industry.

Authorities have not released further information about potential additional charges or upcoming court proceedings for Gledhill at this time.

cards.headline: China restricts content in popular micro dramas
cards.teaser: Chinese authorities are cracking down on soft pornography, violence, and materialistic themes in short-form video dramas.
cards.body:
China has moved to restrict content in micro dramas, the short-form video series that have surged in popularity across the country. Authorities are targeting productions that feature soft pornography, violence, and materialistic themes.

The dramas have drawn criticism for sensationalist content despite their widespread viewership. Chinese regulators have increased scrutiny of the format as it has grown into a major entertainment category.

cards.headline: Kate Winslet surprises blind teenage film fan with phone call
cards.teaser: The Oscar-winning actress called Eryn, a teenager who traveled three hours for an accessible film screening.
cards.body:
Oscar-winning actress Kate Winslet surprised teenager Eryn with a personal phone call after learning about the young film fan's dedication to cinema. Eryn, who has been blind since birth, travelled three hours each way to attend a film screening because no accessible cinema was available locally.

Winslet's thoughtful gesture delighted the enthusiastic moviegoer, recognising the effort Eryn made to pursue their passion for film despite the accessibility barriers they faced.

cards.headline: Phoebe Bridgers performs phone-free acoustic show at Madison Square Garden
cards.teaser: The singer-songwriter played eight new songs at an intimate concert where 18,000 attendees had their phones locked up.
cards.body:
Phoebe Bridgers held a special acoustic concert at Madison Square Garden where approximately 18,000 attendees locked away their phones for the evening. The artist expressed her appreciation for the phone-free environment, remarking on how different it felt without devices in the audience.

During the performance, Bridgers debuted eight new songs. She created an intimate atmosphere in the large venue, transforming the arena into what she described as a living room setting for the acoustic show.

cards.headline: Florida Georgia Line reunite with surprise CMA Fest appearance
cards.teaser: Tyler Hubbard and Brian Kelley performed together at Nissan Stadium in Nashville, signaling the return of the country duo.
cards.body:
Country music duo Florida Georgia Line made a surprise reunion appearance at CMA Fest in Nashville. Tyler Hubbard and Brian Kelley took the stage together at Nissan Stadium, their first joint performance since splitting in 2022.

The appearance signals the return of Florida Georgia Line after a four-year hiatus. The duo had been one of country music's most successful acts before announcing their split.

cards.headline: Taylor Swift releases new song for Toy Story 5
cards.teaser: The singer debuted "I Knew It, I Knew You," co-written and produced with Jack Antonoff, for the upcoming Pixar film.
cards.body:
Taylor Swift has released an original song for Toy Story 5 titled "I Knew It, I Knew You." She co-wrote and produced the track with longtime collaborator Jack Antonoff. The song debuted on digital services Thursday night.

The song centers on Jessie and her reunion with her owner. Swift's contribution marks her involvement in the upcoming Pixar animated film.

cards.headline: CBS correspondent Scott Pelley recounts confronting his boss
cards.teaser: The longtime journalist shared the story of telling off a superior during his career at the network.
cards.body:
Scott Pelley, a veteran 60 Minutes correspondent, was fired by CBS News after clashing with the network's new management. In a public statement, Pelley accused CBS executives of silencing employees and instructing him to inject falsehoods and bias into his reporting.

Pelley emphasized that 60 Minutes built its decades-long reputation as America's top program through integrity, quality, and humanity. His firing has been characterized as a stand for journalistic principles against corporate pressure to compromise editorial standards.

hero.headline: House committee passes $1.15 trillion defense bill after 14-hour session
hero.body:
The House of Representatives voted 312-112 on Wednesday to approve a sweeping defense policy bill that authorizes $900 billion in military programs for the coming year. The 3,000-page legislation, known as the National Defense Authorization Act, includes significant provisions for troop compensation, weapons procurement reforms, and continued support for Ukraine.

The bill provides a 3.8 percent pay raise for many military members and funds improvements to military housing and facilities. It also overhauls how the Department of Defense purchases weapons, emphasizing speed after years of delays from the defense industry.

The legislation maintains a strong U.S. military presence in Europe by requiring the Pentagon to keep at least 76,000 troops and major equipment stationed there unless NATO allies are consulted. The bill also sets a minimum requirement of 28,500 troops in South Korea. Additionally, it authorizes $400 million for each of the next two years to manufacture weapons for Ukraine, demonstrating congressional commitment to supporting the country against Russian aggression.

The bill includes a controversial provision regarding boat strikes in the Caribbean targeting suspected drug smugglers. It demands that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth provide Congress with full, unedited video of a September strike near Venezuela that killed survivors of an earlier strike. The legislation withholds part of Hegseth's travel budget until the Pentagon releases this footage and allows Congress to review the orders for the strikes.

The measure makes significant cuts aligned with the Trump administration's priorities. It reduces climate-related spending by $1.6 billion, reversing years of military investment in addressing climate change as a national security threat. The bill also cuts $40 million in funding for diversity, equity, and inclusion programs.

Congress is formally ending the war in Iraq by repealing the 2003 authorization for the invasion. Supporters say the repeal prevents future abuses and reinforces that Iraq is now a strategic partner. The legislation also permanently removes U.S. sanctions on Syria imposed in 2019, allowing international companies to invest in reconstruction efforts under the new Syrian government.

The bill strikes bipartisan compromises on several issues. While cutting climate and diversity efforts, it boosts congressional oversight of the Pentagon and includes provisions to keep U.S. troops stationed abroad. However, the legislation faced criticism from some senators regarding military flight restrictions over Washington following a deadly midair collision earlier this year between an Army helicopter and a commercial jetliner near Ronald Reagan National Airport.

Democrats criticized Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson for stripping a provision to expand in vitro fertilization coverage for active duty military personnel.

The White House has signaled support for the legislation, which now heads to the Senate for consideration before lawmakers depart for the holiday break.

cards.headline: Senator works to block Trump anti-weaponization fund during budget vote
cards.teaser: Republican and Democratic senators say Bill Cassidy is working to remove a proposed $1.8 billion fund from the budget package.
cards.body:
Senate Republicans narrowly blocked an attempt Thursday to eliminate President Trump's proposed $1.8 billion fund, which would pay his allies. Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer had proposed inserting language into Republican-backed legislation to prevent the payouts, but the measure failed to pass.

The extended vote-a-rama—a marathon series of amendment votes on the budget reconciliation package—revealed divisions within the Republican party, with three GOP senators joining Democrats in opposing the fund. The voting session stretched longer than typical as lawmakers debated the contentious proposal amid signs of internal party dissent over the initiative.

cards.headline: Senate Republicans defeat anti-weaponization fund amendment
cards.teaser: Senate Republicans blocked a Democratic proposal to prohibit the Justice Department from establishing an $1.8 billion fund.
cards.body:
Senate Republicans narrowly blocked a Democratic amendment Thursday that would have prevented President Trump from establishing a $1.8 billion fund to pay his allies. The vote failed 49-50 as Democrats, led by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, attempted to insert language barring the payouts into Republican-backed legislation funding Trump's mass deportation campaign.

The amendment vote occurred during a marathon series of votes on a $70 billion budget reconciliation package. The close margin and signs of dissent within Republican ranks suggest the proposal is exposing divisions within Trump's party over the controversial fund.

cards.headline: FCC reviewing school internet subsidy program over screen time concerns
cards.teaser: The commission announced a review of a $3 billion annual program that provides internet access to schools and libraries.
cards.body:
The Federal Communications Commission is conducting a comprehensive review of the E-Rate program, which distributes $3 billion annually to help schools and libraries access affordable internet. FCC Chair Brendan Carr announced the initiative Wednesday, citing health concerns related to excessive screen time among children.

The E-Rate program has long served as a critical funding mechanism for educational institutions seeking to maintain internet connectivity. Carr's announcement signals the agency's intention to examine the program's current impact and release findings on the screen time issue.

cards.headline: Former Interior Secretary Haaland wins New Mexico Democratic primary for governor
cards.teaser: Deb Haaland, who served in the Biden administration, secured the Democratic nomination in New Mexico's gubernatorial race.
cards.body:
Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland won the Democratic primary for governor of New Mexico on Thursday. The former cabinet member from the Biden administration is now advancing to the November general election, where she will face the Republican nominee.

If elected, Haaland would make history as the first female Native American governor in the country.

cards.headline: Xavier Becerra advances in California governor race
cards.teaser: The former Health and Human Services secretary secured a spot in November's general election to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom.
cards.body:
Former Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra advanced Thursday to the November general election in California's gubernatorial race. Trump-backed Fox News commentator Steve Hilton and billionaire Tom Steyer are competing for the second spot on the November ballot.

California uses a top-two primary system, where the two candidates with the most votes advance to the general election regardless of party affiliation. Becerra is seeking to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom.

cards.headline: Susan Collins casts 10,000th consecutive Senate vote
cards.teaser: The Maine senator maintained her perfect voting attendance record with a vote on a budget package amendment Thursday night.
cards.body:
Sen. Susan Collins cast her 10,000th consecutive Senate vote Thursday night, voting for a Democratic motion to send the $70 billion budget reconciliation package back to the Judiciary Committee. Collins stood at her desk and announced her vote when the clerk called her name.

The Maine Republican has maintained a perfect voting attendance record throughout her Senate career. The milestone came during a lengthy voting session on amendments to the budget reconciliation package.
